text.title: **The Disciplined Operator**
text.subtitle: Trader's Operating System · Module 3 · 41:41
text.body: The course as it is in the store today: eight clip files, the cards as drawn in 2026-05

segments.label: The Pathologies Every Operator Carries
segments.status: AS PUBLISHED: course 0–200 s; the player card's text is kept in `why`
segments.why:
*"Words never spoken … manifests in each of us as human beings."*

Tom Hardison and Ken open with rigidity and revenge — the two psychological pathologies that show up in every trader's day, on the road, on the soccer sideline, at the desk.

segments.label: The Stupid Gate Story
segments.status: AS PUBLISHED: course 200–380 s; the player card's text is kept in `why`
segments.why: Tom's microcosm: the same military-base gate he's driven through for 27 years still produces a flash of [col5:rigidity + revenge]. The lesson — the patterns are lifelong. Operating yourself means [col5:managing them], not eliminating them.

segments.label: Tonight We Get to Explore
segments.status: AS PUBLISHED: course 380–450 s; the player card's text is kept in `why`
segments.why: Ken's coaching move: do not fix today. Explore. The discipline of the operator starts with the willingness to look at the pathology without flinching.

text.title: Chapter 1b — Take the Wheel
text.body: Four and a half minutes. The interruption discipline. When you notice the monkey is driving, what do you do?

segments.label: How Long Are You Going to Watch the Monkey Drive?
segments.status: AS PUBLISHED: course 452–600 s; the player card's text is kept in `why`
segments.why:
*"How long are you going to watch the monkey drive? You know that's wrong."*

The central question of the chapter. Awareness is not enough — there is a taking-over move the operator has to make.

segments.label: Take the Wheel the Way You Would for Your Kids
segments.status: AS PUBLISHED: course 600–721 s; the player card's text is kept in `why`
segments.why:
*"If it was my kids driving the car in a poor state of mind, I wouldn't hesitate to just take the wheel."*

Ken's reframe: authority over the monkey is not optional. It's the same authority you'd exercise instantly for a child you love. [col5:Stop. Flip. Drive.]

text.title: Chapter 2 — The Soccer Game
text.body: Four minutes. The single cleanest model Ken has for what a trade actually is — borrowed from the sideline of his daughter's games.

segments.label: Protect the Goal First
segments.status: AS PUBLISHED: course 721–830 s; the player card's text is kept in `why`
segments.why:
*"Can we protect our goal?"*

The first phase of every trade. Protection against disaster — the [col5:1R loss ceiling] — gets set before anything else happens. Risk box up, mental commitment to honor it.

segments.label: ★ Then Get the Ball
segments.status: AS PUBLISHED: course 830–880 s; the player card's text is kept in `why`
segments.why:
*"Now that we've protected our goal, can we get the ball?"*

Phase two: stalking — preparing to enter, knowing how to win the ball, [col5:making the entry in the direction of price at exactly the right moment, stepping in and taking possession].

segments.label: Go to the Goal — Find Space, Stay Out of Congestion
segments.status: AS PUBLISHED: course 880–940 s; the player card's text is kept in `why`
segments.why: Phase three: execution. "That path is supposed to find space and stay away from congestion. Let the thing run with speed." The trade is in flight; you protect what it's doing rather than over-manage it.

segments.label: Shoot and Score
segments.status: AS PUBLISHED: course 940–959 s; the player card's text is kept in `why`
segments.why:
Phase four: delivery. *"Can I shoot and score? Can I deliver the result that's indicated?"*

The exit. Every trade has all four phases. Skipping one is how trades die.

text.title: Chapter 3 — Aristotle's Spectrum
text.body: Seven minutes. Why pride is the most dangerous failure mode, and where judgment sits on the spectrum.

segments.label: Pride Is the First Deadly Sin
segments.status: AS PUBLISHED: course 961–1120 s; the player card's text is kept in `why`
segments.why:
*"Of the seven deadly sins, pride is the first most dangerous one."*

Not greed. Not fear. Pride — because pride is what makes the trader ignore the data and override the system.

segments.label: Aristotle Puts Judgment in the Middle
segments.status: AS PUBLISHED: course 1120–1280 s; the player card's text is kept in `why`
segments.why:
*"What Aristotle would say is on the spectrum, judgment is in the middle. Confidence is in the middle."*

To the right: overconfidence → pride. To the left: [col5:unconfidence → fear → self-doubt → timidity]. The operator's job is to live in the middle and recognize the slip in either direction.

segments.label: Both Failure Modes Cost the Same
segments.status: AS PUBLISHED: course 1280–1370 s; the player card's text is kept in `why`
segments.why: Pride kills via overreach. Timidity kills via missed trades and undersized winners. The disciplined operator tracks his own position on the spectrum the way he tracks the chart.

text.title: Chapter 3b — The A/B/C Game
text.body: Four minutes. The scoring system that turns the confidence spectrum into actionable session feedback.

segments.label: The B Game Is Your Center of Mass
segments.status: AS PUBLISHED: course 1372–1450 s; the player card's text is kept in `why`
segments.why:
*"The normal game, the B game, is zero plus or minus one [sigma]."*

Ken's grading frame: most of your sessions are B. The B-game band is Z minus one to Z plus one — one standard deviation either side of your personal mean.

segments.label: ★ Z+1 Is Where the A Game Begins
segments.status: AS PUBLISHED: course 1450–1530 s; the player card's text is kept in `why`
segments.why:
*"Z plus one — that's the boundary. That's where the A game begins."*

The A game is rare and one-sigma above your norm. Below Z minus one is C — the days when the operator is [col5:not himself]. Centered on A and C at the two-sigma extremes.

segments.label: Rate the Session, Not the P&L
segments.status: AS PUBLISHED: course 1530–1631 s; the player card's text is kept in `why`
segments.why: The grade is about how well you ran the system — not whether the day made money. A perfectly executed B-game session is the win condition. Operator hygiene is rating session by session, not month by month.

text.title: Chapter 4 — Three Machine Guns
text.body: Four and a half minutes. An army parable for disciplined firepower — and why your trading system is one too.

segments.label: Three Guns, One Stream of Fire
segments.status: AS PUBLISHED: course 1633–1780 s; the player card's text is kept in `why`
segments.why: Ken's army parable: three machine guns each at 100 rounds per minute in rotation, sounding like one [col5:continuous burst]. Total firepower equals one gun at full rate, but ammunition lasts 20 minutes instead of running dry.

segments.label: Disciplined Fire Wins the Engagement
segments.status: AS PUBLISHED: course 1780–1900 s; the player card's text is kept in `why`
segments.why: The point: rationed firepower outlasts the engagement. Most traders fire 600-rounds-a-minute at every setup and run dry by mid-morning. [col5:Rotate. Pause. Conserve.] The system that survives is the one that fires less, more deliberately.

text.title: Chapter 4b — Cut the Frankenstein
text.body: Four and a half minutes. The opposite of adding more rules — the discipline of cutting until only the essential remains.

segments.label: The Frankenstein Creature
segments.status: AS PUBLISHED: course 1903–2050 s; the player card's text is kept in `why`
segments.why:
*"You're persuading yourself that the software and the robot are doing it, but you're always watching your little Frankenstein creature."*

The pattern Ken sees in technical-analysis programmers: one more rule, one more indicator, one more test. The system grows but the operator [col5:never stops watching it].

segments.label: The Minimum Mission-Essential Set
segments.status: AS PUBLISHED: course 2050–2170 s; the player card's text is kept in `why`
segments.why:
*"What's the minimum mission-essential set of things that I need?"*

The army doctrine inverts retail trader instinct. Cut indicators. Cut rules. Cut steps. The system that requires the least monitoring is the strongest one.

text.title: Chapter 5 — Portfolio Heat
text.body: Five and a half minutes. The book-level risk number every operator must be able to name in seconds.

segments.label: Define It Before You Need It
segments.status: AS PUBLISHED: course 2173–2330 s; the player card's text is kept in `why`
segments.why:
*"What's your total portfolio heat? Describe that in terms of a number."*

Ken's coaching with Tom: the operator who can't name his portfolio heat in a number cannot manage it. The number is the sum of open risk across all positions [col5:if every one failed at the same time].

segments.label: ★ Portfolio Heat Is System-Level Risk
segments.status: AS PUBLISHED: course 2330–2440 s; the player card's text is kept in `why`
segments.why:
*"And I summed all of the open risk, and then if all of those trades failed at the same time. That's portfolio heat."*

Not the worst-case loss on the worst trade. The worst-case loss across the whole book in a single bad day. The number every disciplined operator monitors at all times.

segments.label: Dynamic Risk Threshold
segments.status: AS PUBLISHED: course 2440–2499 s; the player card's text is kept in `why`
segments.why: Heat is expressed as a percentage of total risk capital — not raw dollars. The threshold is dynamic: it tightens in drawdown, loosens after wins. Sizing the next trade is always sizing against [col5:remaining heat capacity], not absolute dollars.

text.title: Five chapters, one operator.
text.body:
Pathologies named. Wheel taken. Soccer game played. Spectrum tracked. Firepower rationed. Frankenstein cut. Heat measured.
